en: Bl. 157V1–R5: Pūrṇika (SĀ[Hos1] 4).

Then the venerable Pūrṇika, having perceived that many wanderers of other sects had recently departed, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Pūrṇika [related] everything that had occurred regarding those many wanderers of other sects.
He reported to the Blessed One in detail all that had been said during their conversation together, and spoke as follows:
"Venerable Sir, in explaining it in this way, do I not misrepresent the Blessed One? Do I not overstep what has been said?

Am I one who speaks according to the words of the Blessed One, who speaks according to the Dharma, and who explains the Dharma in accordance with the true nature of the Dharma? And may it not be the case that..."
"Suppose someone were to come from elsewhere to engage in a formal debate according to the Dharma—a practice worthy of a householder.

In that case, Pūrṇika, by answering truthfully, you would not be misrepresenting me; you would speak as one who has heard what was said, you would be a speaker of the Dharma, and you would explain the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma. And no one would come against you."
Engaging in debate and counter-debate with others according to the Dharma is a practice characteristic of the household life.

Why is that? Because previously, Pūrṇika... due to a lack of realization, [beings] were born from the womb of dogs, born from molasses and *guñjā* seeds, born from *muñja* and *balbaja* grass; they were caught in the cycle of coming and going, passing from this world to the next world, and from the next world back to this world.
They run about and wander through the cycles of existence, never transcending them.

(8) O Pūrṇika, if false conceptions were to go to complete disappearance, total destruction, and utter exhaustion—being entirely eliminated for the long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness of all living beings—[then that would be so].
Bl. 157R5–159V2: *Kokanada Sūtra* (SĀ(Hos1) 1).

The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground. Then, during the last watch of the night, the Venerable Ānanda rose and went to the Tapodā River. Having approached, he stood on the bank of the Tapodā River.
Having set aside his robes and plunged into the river Tapodā, he bathed his limbs; then, emerging from the river Tapodā, he stood there wearing only a single robe, drying his limbs.
At that time, the wandering mendicant Kokanada approached the river Tapodā. He heard:
The Venerable Ānanda heard the sound of the wandering mendicant Kokanada pouring water. Having heard it, the Venerable Ānanda made a clearing-sound.

The wandering mendicant Kokanada heard that clearing-sound, and having heard it, he spoke thus: "Who is this, venerable sir? "I am a śramaṇa. "Of which śramaṇas? "Of those who are sons of the Śākya. [Kokanada said: "May I ask a question?"
"I, venerable sir, would ask something regarding a certain point, if you would grant me the opportunity to have my question answered. "Ask, venerable sir;
having heard it, I shall explain it to you.
"But, venerable sir, does the Tathāgata exist after death? "The Blessed One has declared this to be undeclared: whether the Tathāgata exists after death."
"After death, does the Tathāgata exist? Or, Venerable One, does he neither exist nor not exist?
Or does he neither exist nor not exist after death? "The Blessed One has not declared that 'after death the Tathāgata exists,' or 'he neither exists nor does not exist.'"
5. "Venerable sir, when asked, 'Does the Tathāgata exist after death?', you say it is undeclared (*avyākṛta*).

When asked, 'Does the Tathāgata not exist after death? Does he both exist and not exist after death? Does he neither exist nor not exist after death?', you say it is undeclared. But, venerable sir, is it that you do not know or do not see? "I do not."
"Venerable sir, I do not know; I do not see. "I do know; I do see. "But what, venerable sir, do you know? What do you see?

"View, the basis for view, and the station of view—this I know; this I see. And in this way, venerable sir, I know; in this way I see. What then is it that I do not know? What is it that I do not see?"
"Who is this, venerable Ānanda? "It is wonderful that there is such a conversation between a great teacher and his disciple!
If I had recognized him as the venerable Ānanda, I would have displayed such eloquence; alas, sir! Having said this, he departed.
Folio 159V2–162V1: Anāthapiṇḍada (SĀ[Hos1] 1).

The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada. Now at that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went out from Śrāvastī during the day in order to see the Blessed One and to attend upon the Blessed One.

2. Then this thought occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada: "It is still too early for me to go to see the Blessed One and to attend upon the Blessed One; the Blessed One and the monks are in retreat. What if I were to go to where the park of the other non-Buddhist wanderers is located?"
3. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to the park of the wanderers of other sects.
Having approached and exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the wanderers of other sects, he sat down to one side.

4. Then the wandering mendicants of other sects said this: "Householder, you speak of the view of the ascetic Gautama. What is Gautama’s view? What does Gautama see? [The householder replied: "Sirs, even I do not know what the Blessed One’s view is or what the Blessed One sees. In that case, householder, you speak of the view of the community of monks. What is the community of monks’ [view]?"

“Vision—what does it see, O Saṃgha of monks? “I too do not know, sirs, what the vision of the Saṃgha of monks is, nor what the Saṃgha of monks sees. “In that case, householder, what is the vision of a householder? What does a householder see? “Well then, sirs, first explain each your own vision; afterwards, you may explain my vision.”
"It will not be difficult.
Then, a certain wandering ascetic of another sect said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"My view is that the world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is delusion. Another said thus: "My view is that the world is non-eternal..."

In this world, some say: "This is the truth, everything else is delusion. Others say: "The world is both eternal and non-eternal. Others say: "The world is neither eternal nor non-eternal. [Some say: "The world is finite; it is infinite; it is both finite and infinite;
it is neither finite nor infinite. [Some say: "The soul is the same as the body; the soul is one thing and the body another. It exists.

“The Tathāgata exists after death; he does not exist; he both exists and does not exist; or he neither exists nor does not exist after death. Another said this: “My view is that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. This alone is the truth; all else is delusion.
Then other wandering ascetics of other sects said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada: “Householder, we each proclaim our own respective views. Householder, please state yours: what is your view?”
"What does vision see?
"Householder, my vision sees what is real, conditioned, volitional, and dependently originated.
That which is real, conditioned, volitional, and dependently originated is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering. Thus [he spoke].
Having understood this, I have therefore not accepted this view in any way whatsoever.
[The view that] "the world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this view is something real, conditioned, volitional, and dependently originated;
for whatever is real, conditioned, volitional, and dependently originated...

That which is impermanent is suffering. Therefore, this venerable one is attached to suffering alone; he has fully accepted suffering alone; he is settled in suffering alone; he has entered into suffering alone. (9) ... [He who] speaks thus: "The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—such is his fault. As before, up to...

"Neither does the Tathāgata exist after death, nor does he not exist after death. This is the truth; anything else is delusion. This view is real, conditioned, volitional, and dependently originated. Whatever is real, conditioned, volitional, and dependently originated is impermanent; whatever is impermanent is suffering. Therefore, this venerable one is suffering.

Thus he is clinging; he is fully committed to suffering alone; he is settled in suffering alone; he has entered into suffering alone. ... [One who] speaks thus: "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death—this is the truth, and any other view is delusion.
Then, a certain wandering ascetic of another sect said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada: "Is it not so?"

The householder’s view is also that what is real, conditioned, volitional, and dependently originated—whatever is real, conditioned, volitional, and dependently originated—is impermanent; and whatever is impermanent is suffering. Therefore, the householder too is attached to suffering alone, has clung to suffering alone, is settled upon suffering alone, and has entered into suffering alone.

"11. 'Sirs, my view is this: that which is real, conditioned, volitional, and dependently originated—whatever is real, conditioned, volitional, and dependently originated—that is impermanent; and whatever is impermanent—that is suffering.
Having understood this, I have therefore not accepted this view in any way whatsoever. It is just so, householder."

12. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having refuted the arguments of the wanderers of other sects in the park, having illuminated his own doctrine, and having let out a lion’s roar in the assembly, rose from his seat and departed. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Anāthapiṇḍada—
The householder reported in detail to the Blessed One everything that had occurred, including his conversation with many wandering mendicants of other sects.
When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada: "Excellent, excellent, householder! It is good for one to speak from time to time..."
Folio 162V2–166R5: Dīrghanakha SĀ(Hos2) 1.

The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Then the wandering mendicant Dīrghanakha approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, words of mutual courtesy and cordiality.
Having concluded their various conversations, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wandering mendicant Dīrghanakha said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Gautama, nothing is acceptable to me. Even this of yours—"
Agnivaiśyāyana, this view is not acceptable to me: namely, the view that "nothing is acceptable to me," even this very view of mine— "nothing is acceptable to me"— is not acceptable to me.
"Furthermore, Agnivaiśyāyana, for one who knows thus and sees thus, will there be the abandonment, relinquishment, and disappearance of this view,
as well as the non-reconnection, non-clinging, and non-manifestation of another view? Yes, indeed, Master Gautama."
For one who knows thus and sees thus, there will be the abandoning, the relinquishing, and the disappearance of this view;
and there will be the non-relinking, the non-grasping, and the non-manifestation of another view.
By many people, you—

"Agnivaiśyāyana, there will be a convergence of views; many people will come to hold such a view and speak in such a manner. You too would be just like them, Agnivaiśyāyana—whosoever they may be, whether śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
They relinquish this view and do not adopt another view. These are called the ascetics or brahmins who are thinner than the thin in the world.
5. Agnivaiśyāyana, there are these three bases for views. Which three? Here, Agnivaiśyāyana—

One person has such a view and speaks thus: "Everything is acceptable to me. Furthermore, another person here has such a view and speaks thus: "Nothing is acceptable to me. Furthermore, another person here has such a view and speaks thus: "Some things are acceptable to me, and some things are not acceptable to me."

6. In this regard, Agnivaiśyāyana, as for this view: "Everything is acceptable to me"—this view leads to passion, not to the absence of passion; it leads to aversion, not to the absence of aversion; it leads to delusion, not to the absence of delusion; it leads to bondage, not to the absence of bondage; it leads to affliction, not to purification; it leads to accumulation, not to diminution.
It leads to delighting in, grasping, and clinging.
7. This view, "Nothing is acceptable to me," leads to non-attachment, not to attachment; it leads to non-hatred, not to hatred.
For the sake of non-delusion, not for delusion; for the sake of non-attachment, not for attachment;
for the sake of purification, not for defilement.
It leads neither to accumulation nor to non-accumulation; it leads to non-delight, non-clinging, and non-adherence.
In this regard, Agnivaiśyāyana, as for this view: "In one respect I find it acceptable; in another respect I do not find it acceptable"—that which...
In this regard, whatever is agreeable to him conduces to passion and not to the absence of passion, and so on as before, up to: it conduces to attachment;
whereas whatever is disagreeable to him conduces to the absence of passion and not to passion, and so on as before, up to:
it conduces to the absence of attachment.
9. In this regard, the learned noble disciple trains himself thus: "If I were to hold such a view and speak thus:

'Everything is acceptable to me,' then I would have conflict and dispute with two [types of people]: with one who holds such a view and speaks thus, 'Nothing is acceptable to me'; and with one who holds such a view and speaks thus, 'Some things are acceptable to me.'"

"It is not acceptable to me that there should be conflict; for when there is conflict, there is dispute, and when there is dispute, there is violence. Thus, perceiving conflict, dispute, and violence, he relinquishes this view and does not take up another view. In this way, for him...
And there is the abandoning of that view, its relinquishment, its exhaustion, and the non-reconnection, non-grasping, and non-manifestation of another view.
In this regard, the learned noble disciple trains himself thus:

If I were to hold such a view and speak thus: "Nothing is acceptable to me," I would have conflict and dispute with two [positions]: with one who holds the view and speaks thus, "Everything is acceptable to me," and with one who holds the view and speaks thus, "Some things are acceptable to me, while some things are not acceptable to me."
When there is dispute, there is contention; when there is contention, there is violence—and as before, up to: no rebirth-linking, no grasping, and no manifestation.
In this regard, the learned noble disciple trains himself thus:
"If I were to hold such a view and speak in such a way..."
"One thing is acceptable to me, while another is not acceptable to me;
there would be conflict and dispute for me with two [others]: namely, one who holds such a view and speaks thus, and [another] for whom everything is acceptable to me."

It is permissible for one who holds such a view and speaks thus: "Nothing whatsoever is acceptable to me. When there is conflict, there is dispute, as previously described, up to: no reconnection, no grasping, and no manifestation.
Indeed, Agnivaiśyāyana, this body—material, gross, composed of the four great elements—is [regarded] by the noble disciple...
One should dwell constantly contemplating impermanence, contemplating passing away, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation,
and contemplating relinquishment. For a noble disciple who dwells thus— contemplating impermanence, contemplating passing away,
contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment— whatever [feeling] arises for him...
There is desire for the body, affection for the body, love for the body, attachment to the body, clinging to the body, and obsession with the body; yet his mind does not remain overwhelmed by that.
13. Agnivaiśyāyana, there are these three feelings. Which three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and [neutral feeling].
And there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Thus, what is the source of these three feelings? What is their origin? What is their birth? What is their arising?
These feelings have contact as their source, contact as their origin, contact as their birth, and contact as their arising.
With the arising of this or that contact, those respective feelings arise. With the cessation of this or that contact, those [feelings cease].

Those feelings cease, become stilled, grow cool, and vanish. Whatever feeling he experiences— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— he understands the arising and the passing away of those feelings, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them.

And he understands them as they truly are. Understanding, as they truly are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding those feelings, he dwells observing impermanence in those arisen feelings;
he dwells observing their vanishing, observing their fading away, observing their cessation, and observing their relinquishment.

15. Experiencing a feeling that has the body as its limit, he understands, as it truly is, "I am experiencing a feeling that has the body as its limit. Experiencing a feeling that has life as its limit, he understands, as it truly is, "I am experiencing a feeling that has life as its limit. And after the breaking up of the body, upon the exhaustion of life, all [his perceptions] right here...
Feelings cease without remainder; they go to complete cessation, total destruction, and utter exhaustion.
It occurs to him: "Even when experiencing a pleasant feeling, upon the breakup of the body, this will be the end of suffering.
Even when experiencing a painful feeling or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, upon the breakup of the body, this will be the end of suffering."
This indeed is the end of suffering. He experiences even pleasant feeling detached, not bound;

he experiences even painful feeling and even neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling detached, not bound. Detached from what? Detached from passion, hatred, and delusion; detached from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
"I say that one who is disjoined from suffering is [liberated].

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having been ordained for half a month, was standing behind the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One. Then, this thought occurred to the Venerable Śāriputra:

It occurred thus: the Blessed One praised only the abandonment of those phenomena; he praised only dispassion, only cessation, and only relinquishment. Then, as the venerable Śāriputra dwelt contemplating the impermanence of these phenomena, contemplating their passing away, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment—
As he dwelt thus, his mind was liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
And for the wandering mendicant Dīrghanakha, the dustless, stainless eye of Dharma arose regarding all phenomena.
Then the wandering mendicant Dīrghanakha had seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma.
Having crossed over doubt, having transcended uncertainty, no longer dependent on others, not led by another, and having attained confidence in the teachings of the Master regarding all phenomena,
he rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."

"I shall practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Blessed One. Thus did the wandering mendicant Dīrghanakha obtain the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. Having thus gone forth, that venerable one—for the sake of which sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don saffron robes, and with right faith depart from the home—[practiced the holy life.]
They went forth into the homeless life. As before, up until he became an Arhat with a mind well-liberated. ...
"Now, as you know, ... was there a connection with Śāriputra? ... [he asked].

Folios 167V1–170V3: Śarabha SĀ(Hos3) 1. The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Now at that time, a wandering mendicant named Śarabha was residing at Rājagṛha on the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus pond. [...]
He spoke these words in the assembly: "I have understood the Dharma of the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas. Having understood it, I have departed from that Dharma and Vinaya.
Then, a great number of monks, having dressed in the forenoon and taken their bowls and robes, entered Rājagṛha for alms.

They entered. A great many monks, while wandering for alms in Rājagṛha, heard that a wandering ascetic named Śarabha was residing in this Rājagṛha, and that he speaks these words in his assembly, as before. Having heard this, and having again wandered for alms in Rājagṛha, they finished their meal and, after their meal, with their alms-bowl [cleaned], [they departed].
Having returned, set aside their bowls and robes, and washed their feet, they approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the many bhikṣus said this to the Blessed One.

3. "Venerable sir, here we, a great number of monks, having dressed in the forenoon and taken our bowls and robes, entered Rājagṛha for alms. While we, a great number of monks, were walking for alms in Rājagṛha, we heard that a wandering mendicant named Śarabha resides in this Rājagṛha, and that he speaks these words in the assembly: [text continues]"
As before. "It would be well, Blessed One, if you would approach the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus pond out of compassion. The Blessed One consented to the many monks by remaining silent.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from his seclusion and went to where the wanderer Śarabha was at the Sumāgadhā [pond].
He approached the bank of the Puṣkariṇī pond. From afar, the wanderer Śarabha saw the Blessed One.

Having seen him, he prepared a seat for the Blessed One and said, "May the Blessed One sit upon this seat that has been prepared. The Blessed One sat down on the seat that had been prepared. Having sat down, the Blessed One [addressed] Śarabha.
He said this to the wanderer:
"Is it true, Śarabha, that you speak thus:
'I have understood the Dharma of the ascetics, the sons of the Śākyas; having understood it, I have departed from that Dharma and Vinaya'?"

6. When this had been said, the wanderer Śarabha remained silent. [The Buddha said: “Śarabha, why are you silent? If your [view] is complete, we shall approve it; if it is incomplete, we shall complete it for you. Yet even now, the wanderer Śarabha remains silent.
Thus he remained silent. A second and even a third time, Śarabha the wanderer remained silent.
Then Śarabha’s own fellow religious practitioners said this to Śarabha the wanderer:
"The very reason you approached the ascetic Gautama was precisely because that ascetic Gautama..."
Having approached, he spoke thus: "Explain it! Explain it! ... If it is complete for you, we shall rejoice in it; if it is incomplete for you, we shall complete it for you.
Śarabha, why are you silent? ... Even now, the wanderer Śarabha remained silent, and a second time he remained silent.
Even for a third time, Śarabha the wanderer remained silent.

Then the Blessed One said this to Śarabha the wanderer: "If anyone were to say of me, 'The ascetic Gautama is not a Tathāgata, a perfectly awakened one,' I would thoroughly and properly cross-examine him and pursue him with inquiry. As he is being thoroughly and properly cross-examined..."

One might resort to one thing while seeking another externally, manifesting anger, malice, and resentment. Or one might become silent, dejected, with shoulders slumped, head bowed, lacking confidence, and lost in deep reflection—just as you are now, Śarabha.
If someone were to say this to me: "The Dharma and Discipline of the ascetic Gautama is not [correct],"... [the rest of the passage continues].

I would thoroughly and properly cross-examine and interrogate him, just as before, up to: "Just as you do now, Śarabha. If anyone were to say to me, "A disciple of the ascetic Gautama is not well-practiced," I would thoroughly and properly cross-examine and interrogate him, just as before, up to: "Just as you do now, Śarabha."...
10. Then the Blessed One, having let out a true lion’s roar in the assembly on the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus-pool, rose from his seat and departed.

11. Then Śarabha the wandering mendicant’s own fellow-celibates said this to Śarabha the wandering mendicant: “For example, Śarabha, it would be as if a bull whose horns have been broken were to think he should let out a great roar in an empty cow-pen.”

In just this way, you think that you should roar the lion’s roar in the assembly before anyone other than the ascetic Gautama. It is just as when a female *śarabha* deer, thinking "I shall utter the cry of a male," utters only the cry of a female *bhaḍḍalikā*. You are not like a *bhaḍḍalikā*;
rather, you think that you should roar the lion’s roar in the assembly before anyone other than the ascetic Gautama. It is just as...

"Like a śarabha deer or a jackal who thinks, 'I shall let out the roar of a bheruṇḍa,' yet lets out only the cry of a jackal; even so do you, apart from the ascetic Gautama, imagine yourself capable of the lion’s roar in this assembly. Then the fellow religious practitioners of the wandering mendicant Śarabha... rose from their seats and departed. This is the Sūtra of Śarabha.

Folio 170V3–172V2: Pīṭha SĀ(Hos3) 1. The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandakanivāpa. Now at that time, a wandering mendicant named Pīṭha was residing in Rājagṛha near the Sumāgadhā lotus pond—here always...

On the bank of the Puṣkariṇī pond, he spoke these words in the assembly: “... whoever shall sing that verse in response to my song, in his presence I will lead the holy life. 2. Then, many monks, having dressed in the forenoon and taken their bowls and robes, entered Rājagṛha for alms. While wandering for alms in Rājagṛha, those many monks heard [the following]:
In this city of Rājagṛha, on the bank of the Puṣkariṇī pond at Sumāgadhā, there lived a wandering mendicant named Pīṭha.
He spoke these words in the assembly, as before. Sitting to one side, the many monks who were seated to one side said this to the Blessed One:
3. "In this matter, Venerable Sir, it is as before. The Blessed One consented to the many monks by remaining silent.

4. Then, in the late afternoon, the Blessed One rose from his seclusion and went to where the wanderer Pīṭha was on the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus pond. The wanderer Pīṭha saw the Blessed One from afar.

Having seen him, he prepared a seat for the Blessed One and said, "May the Blessed One sit upon this seat that has been prepared. The Blessed One sat down upon the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to the wanderer Pīṭha:
"Is it true, indeed, Pīṭha?"
"You speak thus: 'If anyone should sing along with this verse that I have sung, I will practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in his presence. ... I shall sing along with that verse.
Then Pīṭha the wandering mendicant, having placed one stool upon another stool... at that time, he spoke this verse:
... he would not harm any living beings; [he would not cause] any evil deed toward anyone... being restrained in three areas...
7. Then the Blessed One, having understood with his own mind the thought of the wandering mendicant Pīṭha, at that time spoke this verse:

Whatever [is] ... and whatever [is], all that is impermanent; having understood this as it truly is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with suffering. This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
...and do not harm living beings. Who...
he for whom there is no misdeed by body, speech, or mind, being restrained in these three places...

8. Then it occurred to the wandering mendicant Pīṭha: "The ascetic Gautama perceives my mind with his own mind. ... Bowing with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, he addressed the Blessed One as follows:
9. "Venerable Gautama, may I receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
He obtained the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within that well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. Having thus gone forth,

the wandering mendicant Pīṭha became one for whose sake sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don saffron robes, and with right faith go forth from the home to the homeless life— as described previously— until he became an Arhat.
"One whose mind is well-liberated. This is the Sūtra on the Seat (Pīṭha).
Bl. 172V2–173R5: The Truths of the Brahmins (Brāhmaṇasatyāni), SĀ(Hos3) 1.

The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground. Now, while a great number of brahmin wanderers were seated and assembled on the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus pond, this kind of conversation arose among them:
"Such are the truths of the Brahmins; such are the truths of the Brahmins.

The Blessed One heard those many Brahmin wanderers seated and gathered together on the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus pond, engaged in this kind of conversation as they passed the time during their daytime stay.
With the divine ear, purified and surpassing that of humans, he heard [them]. Having heard it, he then went to the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus pond.

A great number of brahmins and wandering mendicants saw the Blessed One from afar. Upon seeing him, they prepared a seat for the Blessed One and said, "May the Blessed One sit upon this seat that has been prepared."
The Blessed One sat down on the very seat that had been prepared. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the many brahmins and wanderers:

"What, indeed, was the conversation among you many brahmins and wanderers as you were sitting together and gathered on the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus pond? And with what topic are you now seated here?"

We have gathered here. Venerable Gautama, while we—a great many brahmin wanderers—were seated together and assembled on the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus pond, this kind of conversation arose among us: "Such are the truths of the brahmins; such are the truths of the brahmins. Venerable Gautama, this was our discussion as a great many of us...

While the brahmins and wanderers were seated and gathered together on the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus pond, their conversation was interrupted. [The Buddha said: "O Gautama, regarding that for which we are now seated and gathered together—there are these three truths of the brahmins (*brāhmaṇasatya*), which have been proclaimed by me after having personally realized, witnessed, and attained them. What are the three?"

6. The brahmins speak thus: "All living beings are not to be killed"—speaking in this way, the brahmins speak the truth and not falsehood. They think, "We are superior," they think, "We are equal," or they think, "We are inferior. Without being attached to whatever truth there may be in this, they dwell in all the world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*). This...
First is the truth of a brahmin: that which has been realized, witnessed, attained, and proclaimed by me through my own direct knowledge.

7. The brahmins speak thus: "Whatever is of the nature of arising, all that is of the nature of cessation. Speaking thus, the brahmins speak the truth and not falsehood. As before, up to: "Not being attached to whatever truth there is herein..."
They dwell observing the arising and passing away in all the world. This is the second brahmin truth, which I have realized for myself, witnessed, attained, and proclaimed.
8. The brahmins say thus: "In me, there is nothing anywhere, belonging to anyone; in him, there is nothing anywhere, belonging to anyone."
“‘There is something’—when the brahmins speak thus, they speak the truth and not falsehood. As before, up to this point:

whatever here is true, by not being attached to that, they dwell without the sense of ‘mine’ in the entire world. This is the third truth of the brahmins, which I have realized for myself, witnessed, attained, and proclaimed.”
